standard_text: Endocrine glands and their hormones (hypothalamus, pituitary, thyroid, pancreas, adrenal glands, ovaries and testes); negative feedback; homeostatic control of blood glucose (insulin and glucagon), water balance (ADH), salt, carbon dioxide and body temperature; diabetes. (summary of the senior secondary Biology curriculum, SSS 3; WAEC and NECO syllabuses)
meta_desc: Free SSS 3 Biology worksheets (senior secondary curriculum, WAEC and NECO): endocrine glands, hormones and their roles, feedback and homeostasis, thermoregulation and blood glucose. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment constant.
body_html:
How to think about it

Hormones are chemical messengers made by endocrine glands and carried in the blood. The pituitary gland controls other glands; the thyroid makes thyroxin (metabolism); the adrenal glands make adrenalin (fight or flight); the pancreas makes insulin and glucagon.

Homeostasis uses negative feedback: when blood glucose rises, insulin makes the liver change glucose to glycogen; when it falls, glucagon makes the liver change glycogen to glucose. ADH controls water balance. When you are too hot, you sweat and blood vessels in the skin dilate (vasodilation); when you are too cold, you shiver and they constrict.

Example

Blood glucose is high after a meal. Which hormone is released?

From the pancreas

Answer: insulin

Example

Which hormone prepares the body for fight or flight?

Adrenal glands

Answer: adrenalin

Common mistakes

  • Thinking insulin is an enzyme.
  • Mixing up glucagon and glycogen.
  • Thinking hormones act as fast as nerves.

faq.a: The pancreas makes little or no insulin, so the blood glucose level is too high; it is treated with insulin injections.

faq.q: Why do your hands look pale on a cold day?
faq.a: Blood vessels in the skin constrict (vasoconstriction) to reduce heat loss.

items.q: How do steroid hormones act on target cells?
c: they enter the cell and bind receptors inside, changing gene expression
items.e: e.g. cortisol and oestrogen.

items.q: Which gland secretes ANF?
c: the Leydig cells of the testis
the atrial wall of the heart
items.e: ANF is made in the atrial wall of the heart.

items.q: Which gland secretes cortisol?
items.e: Cortisol is made in the adrenal cortex.

items.q: Which gland secretes thymosins?
items.e: Thymosins is made in the thymus.

items.q: Which gland is called the master gland?
items.e: It controls many other glands, though the hypothalamus controls it.

items.q: What is the role of glucocorticoids such as cortisol?
c: raising blood glucose (gluconeogenesis) and suppressing inflammation
items.e: They are made in the adrenal cortex.

items.q: Which gland secretes thyrocalcitonin?
items.e: Thyrocalcitonin is made in the thyroid.

items.q: Which gland secretes thyroxine?
c: the Leydig cells of the testis
items.e: Thyroxine is made in the thyroid.

items.q: Which gland secretes parathyroid hormone?
c: the posterior pituitary (made in the hypothalamus)
items.e: Parathyroid hormone is made in the parathyroid glands.

items.q: Which gland secretes adrenaline?
c: the Leydig cells of the testis
items.e: Adrenaline is made in the adrenal medulla.

items.q: Which hormone controls the secretion of gastric juice?
items.e: It is made by the stomach wall.

items.q: Which gland secretes glucagon?
c: the Leydig cells of the testis
items.e: Glucagon is made in the pancreas (α-cells).

items.q: Which hormone is called the 'fight or flight' hormone?
items.e: It raises heartbeat and blood glucose.

items.q: Which gland secretes insulin?
c: the posterior pituitary (made in the hypothalamus)
items.e: Insulin is made in the pancreas (β-cells).

items.q: Which hormone is called the hormone of pregnancy?
items.e: It keeps the uterus lining ready.

items.q: Which gland secretes testosterone?
c: the Leydig cells of the testis
items.e: Testosterone is made in the Leydig cells of the testis.

items.q: Which gland secretes melatonin?
c: the Leydig cells of the testis
items.e: Melatonin is made in the pineal gland.

items.q: Which gland secretes oxytocin?
c: the posterior pituitary (made in the hypothalamus)
items.e: Oxytocin is made in the posterior pituitary (made in the hypothalamus).

items.q: Which gland secretes progesterone?
c: the atrial wall of the heart
items.e: Progesterone is made in the corpus luteum.

items.q: Which part of the body controls the pituitary by releasing hormones?
items.e: It links the nervous and endocrine systems.

items.q: Which hormone is responsible for development of T-lymphocytes?
items.e: Thymosins: development of T-lymphocytes.

items.q: What is the main role of growth hormone?
c: the daily (24-hour) rhythm of sleep and wakefulness
items.e: Growth hormone: body growth.

items.q: Which hormone is responsible for lowering blood glucose?
items.e: Insulin: lowering blood glucose.

items.q: Which hormone is responsible for contraction of the uterus during childbirth and milk ejection?
items.e: Oxytocin: contraction of the uterus during childbirth and milk ejection.

items.q: Which hormone is responsible for controlling the basal metabolic rate?
items.e: Thyroxine: controlling the basal metabolic rate.

items.q: What is the main role of ANF?
c: contraction of the uterus during childbirth and milk ejection
raising the Ca²⁺ level in the blood
the daily (24-hour) rhythm of sleep and wakefulness
items.e: ANF: lowering blood pressure.

items.q: What is the main role of parathyroid hormone?
c: raising the Ca²⁺ level in the blood
raising blood glucose and reducing inflammation
items.e: Parathyroid hormone: raising the Ca²⁺ level in the blood.

items.q: Which hormone is responsible for the emergency (fight or flight) response?
items.e: Adrenaline: the emergency (fight or flight) response.

items.q: What is the main role of progesterone?
items.e: Progesterone: maintaining pregnancy.

items.q: Which hormone is responsible for lowering blood pressure?
items.e: ANF: lowering blood pressure.

items.q: Which hormone is responsible for raising blood glucose?
items.e: Glucagon: raising blood glucose.

items.q: Which hormone is responsible for body growth?
items.e: Growth hormone: body growth.

items.q: Which hormone is responsible for the daily (24-hour) rhythm of sleep and wakefulness?
items.e: Melatonin: the daily (24-hour) rhythm of sleep and wakefulness.

items.q: What is the main role of glucagon?
c: the daily (24-hour) rhythm of sleep and wakefulness
items.e: Glucagon: raising blood glucose.

items.q: What is the main role of thymosins?
items.e: Thymosins: development of T-lymphocytes.

items.q: What is the main role of testosterone?
c: contraction of the uterus during childbirth and milk ejection
items.e: Testosterone: male secondary sexual characters.

items.q: What is the main role of melatonin?
c: the daily (24-hour) rhythm of sleep and wakefulness
contraction of the uterus during childbirth and milk ejection
items.e: Melatonin: the daily (24-hour) rhythm of sleep and wakefulness.

items.q: Which hormone is responsible for raising blood glucose and reducing inflammation?
items.e: Cortisol: raising blood glucose and reducing inflammation.

items.q: What is the main role of oxytocin?
c: contraction of the uterus during childbirth and milk ejection
items.e: Oxytocin: contraction of the uterus during childbirth and milk ejection.

items.q: What is the main role of cortisol?
c: lowering the Ca²⁺ level in the blood
raising blood glucose and reducing inflammation
raising the Ca²⁺ level in the blood
items.e: Cortisol: raising blood glucose and reducing inflammation.

items.q: How do plants respond to light coming from one side?
c: the shoot grows away from light
auxin moves to the shaded side, so cells there elongate and the shoot bends towards the light
cells on the light side grow faster
items.e: This is positive phototropism.

items.q: Which hormone lowers blood glucose?
items.e: It is made by beta cells in the pancreas.

items.q: How does the body reduce heat loss on a cold day?
c: vasoconstriction of skin blood vessels and shivering
items.e: Shivering makes heat by respiration.

items.q: Glucagon released when blood sugar is low is an example of which kind of feedback?
c: positive feedback (it makes the change bigger)
items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.q: Where is the cardiovascular control centre?
items.e: It changes heart rate through the SAN.

items.q: Which is an example of positive feedback?
items.e: Positive feedback amplifies a change.

items.q: How do thermoreceptors help control body temperature?
c: they detect temperature changes in the skin and blood and send signals to the hypothalamus
items.e: They are the receptors in the feedback loop.

items.q: Shivering when you are cold is an example of which kind of feedback?
c: positive feedback (it makes the change bigger)
items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.q: What is the role of the refractory period?
c: it makes impulses travel in one direction and limits their frequency
items.e: Na⁺ channels cannot reopen straight away.

items.q: What is torpor?
c: a short period of lowered body temperature and metabolism to save energy
items.e: Many small marsupials and bats use torpor on cold nights.

items.q: An impulse travels 60 mm along an axon in 0.50 ms. Calculate its speed in m s⁻¹.
Sweating when you are hot is an example of which kind of feedback?
c: positive feedback (it makes the change bigger)
items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.q: What is the difference between nervous and hormonal control?
c: nerves are fast, short-lived and targeted; hormones are slower, longer-lasting and travel in the blood
items.e: Both coordinate responses.

items.q: Fruit ripening faster as ripe fruit releases more ethene is an example of which kind of feedback?
c: positive feedback (it makes the change bigger)
items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.q: Contractions getting stronger during childbirth is an example of which kind of feedback?
c: positive feedback (it makes the change bigger)
items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.q: What is a synapse?
c: a small gap between neurons where neurotransmitters carry the signal
the cell body of a neuron
items.e: Synapses make impulses travel in one direction.

items.q: What do Ca²⁺ ions do in muscle contraction?
c: move tropomyosin away from the binding sites on actin
items.e: Released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

items.q: An impulse travels 25 mm along an axon in 4.0 ms. Calculate its speed in m s⁻¹.
What is ATP used for in muscle contraction?
c: detaching the myosin head from actin and re-cocking it
items.e: ATP hydrolysis gives the energy for the power stroke cycle.

items.q: Insulin released after a meal is an example of which kind of feedback?
c: positive feedback (it makes the change bigger)
items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.q: Blessing's body temperature is 38.5 °C. The body sweats. Why?
c: to lose heat and cool down
to make heat and warm up
items.e: The response opposes the change.

items.q: Why can a core temperature above about 40 °C be dangerous?
c: enzymes and other proteins start to denature, so body processes fail
items.e: This is heatstroke.

items.q: What is the normal core body temperature of a human?
items.e: Enzymes work best near this temperature.

items.q: What is the role of ADH (antidiuretic hormone)?
c: it makes the kidneys remove more water
it makes the collecting ducts more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed
items.e: Released when blood is too concentrated.

items.q: Drinking water when you are thirsty is an example of which kind of feedback?
c: positive feedback (it makes the change bigger)
items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.q: Why do humans sweat more in dry heat than in humid heat to get the same cooling?
c: sweat evaporates easily in dry air; in humid air evaporation is slow and less cooling happens
sweat cannot form in humid air
items.e: Humid heat is more dangerous.

items.q: Nkechi's body temperature is 38.0 °C (normal is about 37 °C). What does the body do?
c: sweating and blood vessels in the skin widen
shivering and blood vessels in the skin narrow
items.e: Negative feedback moves it back toward 37 °C.

items.q: What is homeostasis?
c: changing the internal environment to match the outside
keeping the internal environment within narrow limits
items.e: Body temperature, blood glucose and water balance are examples.

items.q: How do plants reduce water loss in drought?
c: abscisic acid causes the stomata to close
items.e: Abscisic acid is a stress hormone.

items.q: Which receptors detect a rise in blood concentration (osmotic pressure)?
items.e: The pituitary then releases ADH.

items.q: How does fur or feathers reduce heat loss?
c: they absorb heat from the blood
they trap a layer of still air, which is a poor conductor of heat
items.e: Raised hairs trap a thicker layer.

items.q: What is an endotherm?
c: an animal whose temperature matches its surroundings
an animal that keeps its body temperature constant mainly with heat from its own metabolism
items.e: Mammals and birds are endotherms.

items.q: Why is a fever helpful during an infection?
c: it kills all viruses at once
it lowers the body's metabolic rate
a higher temperature slows the growth of some pathogens and speeds up immune responses
items.e: Very high fevers are dangerous.

items.q: Ada's body temperature is 36.2 °C (normal is about 37 °C). What does the body do?
c: sweating and blood vessels in the skin widen
shivering and blood vessels in the skin narrow
items.e: Negative feedback moves it back toward 37 °C.

items.q: What happens to the heart rate during exercise, and why?
c: it rises, to deliver more oxygen and glucose to muscles and remove CO₂
items.e: The medulla detects rising CO₂.

items.q: Femi's body temperature is 36.3 °C. The body shivers. Why?
c: to make heat and warm up
to lose heat and cool down
items.e: The response opposes the change.

items.q: What is negative feedback?
c: a response that reverses a change and returns a variable to its set point
a response that makes a change bigger
items.e: Most homeostatic control is by negative feedback.

items.q: How does the body lose heat on a hot day?
c: sweating and vasodilation of skin blood vessels
items.e: More blood flows near the skin surface.

items.q: Which hormone raises blood glucose?
items.e: It stimulates the liver to break down glycogen.

items.q: How does the spinifex hopping mouse survive with almost no drinking water?
c: its kidneys make very concentrated urine
it stores water in its tail
items.e: Its loop of Henle is very long.

items.q: Which part of the brain controls body temperature?
items.e: It receives information from thermoreceptors.

Where does ultrafiltration happen in the kidney?
items.e: High blood pressure forces small molecules out.

items.q: After a meal, blood glucose rises from 5.5 to 7.7 mmol dm⁻³ in 45 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of increase.
After a meal, blood glucose rises from 4.8 to 10 mmol dm⁻³ in 60 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of increase.
What is negative feedback?
c: a change triggers a larger change
a response that has no effect
a change triggers a response that brings the level back towards normal
items.e: Most homeostasis uses negative feedback.

items.q: Why does glucose appear in the urine of someone with untreated diabetes?
c: the carrier proteins in the proximal tubule cannot reabsorb all of it
items.e: Blood glucose is too high.

items.q: After a meal, blood glucose rises from 5.2 to 6.8 mmol dm⁻³ in 90 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of increase.
What is the main cause of type 1 diabetes?
c: the β cells cannot make insulin
items.e: It is treated with insulin injections.

items.q: What is homeostasis?
c: keeping the internal environment within restricted limits
changing body temperature with the weather
items.e: For example core temperature, blood glucose and water potential.

items.q: After a meal, blood glucose rises from 4.8 to 10 mmol dm⁻³ in 90 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of increase.
After a meal, blood glucose rises from 4.5 to 9.0 mmol dm⁻³ in 30 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of increase.
After a meal, blood glucose rises from 4.5 to 9.0 mmol dm⁻³ in 45 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of increase.
After a meal, blood glucose rises from 5.0 to 8.5 mmol dm⁻³ in 60 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of increase.
What is a taxis?
c: a change in the rate of movement only
a directional movement of a whole organism towards or away from a stimulus
items.e: Kinesis is a non-directional change in speed or turning.

items.q: What does the loop of Henle do?
c: creates a low water potential in the medulla so water can be reabsorbed
items.e: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are pumped out of the ascending limb.
